now, these ten recollections arise based on a mind without subsequent thoughts and a mind without intervals—this is what constitutes certainty.
Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"When all sentient beings approach the time of death, the 'sword-wind' disintegrates their physical forms, and as the suffering of death presses upon them, they experience great terror."

Therefore, upon encountering a virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitra), one should arouse great vigor and maintain the ten recitations with continuous mindfulness; this constitutes superior roots of goodness and will lead to rebirth in the Pure Land.
Furthermore, it is like a person facing an enemy and breaking through their ranks, exerting the full strength of their body all at once;
the goodness of these ten recitations is also like this.

Furthermore, if at the time of death a person gives rise to even a single thought of wrong view or an intensified evil mind, they can immediately overturn the merit of the three realms and enter the evil paths.
Question: "It has already been stated:
'The goodness of ten recitations at the moment of death can overturn the evil karma of a lifetime and enable one to be born in the Pure Land.'"
"I do not yet know for how long these ten recitations last.
He replied: "As it is said in the Sūtra:"
"One hundred and ten births and deaths constitute one *kṣaṇa*, and sixty *kṣaṇas* constitute one thought-moment (*tatkṣaṇa*).
This is a general explanation of the "thought-moment" based on the sūtras and śāstras.
At this time, one understands mindfulness and does not concern oneself with the specific duration of the moment.

One simply recollects Amitābha Buddha—whether by way of general characteristics or specific characteristics—and contemplates according to the object of focus for ten moments of thought. If there is no intermingling with other thoughts or conceptions, this is called "ten recitations" (daśa-smṛti).
Furthermore, it is said:
"The 'ten continuous recitations' is merely a name for a single count used by the noble ones.

One need only accumulate recitations and concentrate the mind, not allowing other matters to distract one, so that the path of karma may be accomplished; once this is achieved, one may simply cease the practice, and there is no need for the trouble of keeping track of the number of counts.
It is further said:
"If one is a long-practitioner of mindfulness, one should mostly rely on this;
if one is a beginner practicing mindfulness, it is also good to keep count."
"This too is based on the sacred teachings.
He asked again:
"Now I wish to rely on the exhortation to practice the *nien-fo san-mei* (Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi); I do not yet know what the characteristics of the mental recitation (*jì-niàn*) are like?"
He replied:
"It is like a person in a vast, desolate wilderness who encounters hostile bandits; they draw their swords and, displaying great valor, come straight toward him with the intent to kill."
This man walked straight on until he saw a river that needed to be crossed; before he had even reached the bank, he had this thought:
"Once I reach the riverbank, shall I take off my clothes to cross?"
If I cross while wearing my clothes,
I fear there will be no time; if I cross having stripped off my clothes, I fear my life may not be spared.
At that time, he focused his mind solely on the means of crossing the river, with no other thoughts or mental states intervening.

The practitioner is likewise: when mindful of Amitābha Buddha, they are like that person thinking of crossing; moment after moment follows upon one another, with no other thoughts or mental states intervening.

One may contemplate the Buddha’s Dharma-body, or the Buddha’s supernormal powers, or the Buddha’s wisdom, or the Buddha’s white tuft between the eyebrows, or the Buddha’s marks and signs of excellence, or the Buddha’s original vows; the same applies to the recitation of his name.
Provided that one can be single-minded and devoted, maintaining continuity without interruption, one will certainly be born before the Buddha.
I now exhort students of future generations: if you wish to realize the two truths, simply knowing that every thought-moment is ungraspable is the gate of wisdom;
being able to bind the mind to its object in continuous succession without interruption is the gate of merit.
Therefore, a sutra says:
"Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas constantly cultivate their minds through merit and wisdom.

If a beginner has not yet been able to shatter the marks of phenomena, they need only rely upon these marks with single-minded devotion; there are none who will not attain rebirth, so one need have no doubts.
He asked again:
"The *Sūtra of Immeasurable Life* states:

'If sentient beings of the ten directions, with a sincere heart of faith and joy, desire to be born in my land, even if they recite the name but ten times, should they not be born there, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.'"

"Now there are people in the world who, having heard this holy teaching, do not apply their minds at all during their present lifetime, intending instead to practice mindfulness only when they are on the verge of death. How can such a thing be?"
He replied:
"This matter is not analogous. Why is that?
The Sūtra says:
"Ten recitations in continuous succession.
This seems as though it would not be difficult.
However, the minds of ordinary people are like wild horses and their consciousnesses are more restless than monkeys; they gallop through the six sense objects, never once coming to rest.
Each person must give rise to faith and cultivate self-restraint in advance, so that habitual practice becomes their nature and their roots of goodness become firm and stable.
As the Buddha told the Great King:
"When a person accumulates virtuous deeds, they will have no evil thoughts at death;
it is like a tree that has previously leaned—the direction it falls must follow its curve."
"When the 'sword-wind' arrives, a hundred sufferings converge upon the body; if one has not previously cultivated this practice in one's heart, how can one manage it at that moment?

Each of you should, as fellow practitioners, form a pact in groups of three or five in advance to mutually instruct and awaken one another when the end of life approaches, reciting the name of Amitābha and vowing to be born in the Land of Peace and Bliss, so that by chanting the name in succession, you may achieve ten recitations."
It is like pressing a wax seal into clay: when the seal is broken, the impression is formed.
At the moment this life is severed, it is precisely the time of birth in the Land of Peace and Bliss.
Once one has entered the stage of the right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), what further cause for anxiety could there be?
"Each of you should weigh this great benefit; why do you not pre-emptively cultivate mindfulness of it?
He asked again:
"All the Mahāyāna sūtras and śāstras state:"
"All sentient beings are ultimately unborn, just like empty space.
If this is so, why did the Bodhisattvas Tianqin and Longshu both vow to be reborn there?
He replied:
"To say that sentient beings are ultimately unborn, like empty space, has two meanings:
first, as seen by ordinary people, there are real sentient beings and real birth-and-death; [the second is that these are ultimately non-existent]."
If one considers the rebirth of a Bodhisattva, it is ultimately like space or like a rabbit's horn.
Second, what is now called "birth" is birth through causes and conditions;
because it is born through causes and conditions, it is a birth that is merely a provisional designation.
Because they arise as mere designations, they are in fact non-arising;
this does not contradict the Great Principle.
It is not like the common person who claims there are real sentient beings or real birth and death.
He asked again:
"Life has a root, which is the source of all burdens.
If one recognizes this fault and abandons life to seek the birthless, there may be a time of liberation."
Now, since you have already been exhorted to be born in the Pure Land, this is precisely to abandon birth and seek birth; how could such births ever come to an end?
He replied:
“Indeed, that Pure Land is the birth of non-birth, which is the pure fundamental vow of the Tathāgata Amitābha.”
It is not like the arising of sentient beings within the three realms of existence, who give rise to love, defilement, and false attachment. Why is this?
For the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is pure and ultimately without arising; what is called "arising" is merely the perspective of those who perceive arising.
He asked again:
"As it was said above:
'One who knows that birth is non-birth shall be born in the highest realm.'"
If that were so, then for those born of inferior capacity who attain rebirth by means of ten recitations, would this not constitute actual birth?
If it were actual birth, one would fall into two doubts:
first, the fear of not attaining rebirth; [and second, the doubt regarding the nature of that rebirth].
"Second, it means that this characteristic is wholesome, yet it cannot serve as a cause for non-arising.
He replied:
"The explanation has three parts:"
First, it is like placing a pure maṇi jewel into turbid water; by the power of the jewel, the water immediately becomes clear and still.

Likewise, even if a person possesses the immeasurable defilements of birth and death, if they hear the name of the Tathāgata Amitābha—the supreme, non-arising, pure jewel—and cast it into their turbid mind, within every thought-moment their sins will be extinguished and their mind purified, whereby they shall immediately attain rebirth.
2. It is like a pure maṇi jewel wrapped in dark-blue or yellow silk; when it is cast into water, the water immediately becomes dark-blue or yellow, exactly matching the color of the object.

In that pure buddha-field, there is the Tathāgata Amitābha, whose name is like a supreme precious jewel wrapped in the silk of immeasurable merit. When this is cast into the "water of the mind" of those who are to be reborn there, how could it not transform their birth into the wisdom of non-arising?
Third, it is also like lighting a fire upon ice: if the fire is fierce, the ice melts; once the ice has melted, the fire is extinguished.

Although those of the lowest grade who attain rebirth do not understand that the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is birthless, they nonetheless form the intention to go to that land by virtue of the power of invoking the Buddha’s name and vow to be born there. Once they have reached the realm of non-arising, the fire of "birth" naturally extinguishes itself.
He asked again:
"Based on which body is it said that one is reborn?
He replied:

"In this realm, among those conventionally designated as persons, one cultivates various gates of practice; the preceding thought acts as the cause for the succeeding thought. Whether it be a person conventionally designated in an impure land or a person conventionally designated in a pure land, they cannot be determined as identical, nor can they be determined as different;
the same applies to the preceding mind and the succeeding mind."
Why is this? If they were determinedly one, there would be no cause and effect; if they were determinedly different, there would be no continuity.
For this reason, although the horizontal and vertical aspects differ, from beginning to end it is one and the same practitioner.
He asked again:
"If merely being able to recite the name of the Buddha can eliminate all obstacles,
then it would be like a person pointing at the moon with their finger— the finger itself should be able to dispel the darkness."
He replied:
“All phenomena differ in myriad ways and cannot be treated as a single uniformity. Why is this?
There are names that are identical to the phenomena themselves, and there are names that are distinct from the phenomena.

Regarding those names that are identical to the phenomena: these include the names and titles of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, the words and phrases of dharanis and incantations, and the chapters and verses of the sutras.
As the words of the incantation say:
"The sun rises in the east, sometimes red, sometimes yellow; even if the rite of prohibition is performed during the hours of You or Hai, the patient shall likewise be healed."
"Furthermore, it is like a person who has been bitten by a dog; if they cauterize the wound with tiger bone ash, the patient is immediately healed.
Should there be no such bone at hand, one may rub the palm of the hand over it while calling out with the mouth:
'Tiger, come!'"
"O Tiger, come!
Upon saying this, the patient was also cured.
Furthermore, if there were someone suffering from cramps in the legs, by cauterizing them with the branches of a papaya tree, the patient would immediately recover.
If there were no papaya, he would warm his hands over a fire and rub [the fruit] while calling out,
"Papaya! Papaya!"
"The patient was also cured;
my own body has experienced this efficacy. Why is this so?"
"Because the name is itself the phenomenon (*dharma*).
As for the case where the name differs from the phenomenon, it is like using a finger to point at the moon.
He asked again:
"If it is true that anyone who merely recites the name of Amitābha can eliminate the darkness of ignorance for sentient beings throughout the ten directions and attain rebirth,
then what is the meaning of those sentient beings who, though they recite the name and maintain mindfulness, still possess ignorance and do not fulfill their aspirations?"
He replied:
"It is because they do not practice in accordance with reality, and thus their names do not correspond to their actual meaning. Why is this so?"
This means not knowing that the Tathāgata is the body of true reality (dharmatākāya), but regarding him as a physical body (rūpakāya).
Furthermore, there are three kinds of non-correspondence:
first, the lack of purity in faith, because it fluctuates between presence and absence.
Second, the mind of faith is not unified, meaning it lacks decisiveness;
third, the mind of faith is not continuous, meaning it is interrupted by other thoughts.
These aspects mutually encompass one another; if they can be made continuous, then that is the single-mindedness of *ekacitta*.
"Simply being able to focus the mind with single-mindedness is itself the pure mind.
To possess these three minds and yet fail to give rise to them—such a thing is impossible.
Within this third major section, there are four points of analysis:
First, distinguishing between the difficult path and the easy path;

second, clarifying the differences between long and short kalpas; third, clarifying that since beginningless time and kalpas, one has dwelt within these three realms and five destinies, riding upon the two types of karma—wholesome and unwholesome—to receive the two retributions of suffering and pleasure, transmigrating without end through countless births;
fourth, establishing this through the testimony of the holy teachings and exhorting future generations to give rise to faith and seek rebirth there.
First, distinguishing between the difficult path of practice and the easy path of practice.
Within this, there are two parts:
first, presenting the two types of paths; [second, explaining their respective characteristics].
2. Question and Answer Explanation.
Having already placed myself within the realm of fire, I truly harbor feelings of fear.

Looking up, I reflect upon the Great Sage’s consolation through the three vehicles; yet the conveyances of the sheep and the deer are provisional expedients for those who have not yet reached their destination. The Buddha rebukes false attachments that obstruct the supreme quest for Bodhi; even if one later turns toward it, it is still termed a circuitous path.
If one were to directly climb onto the great carriage, that too would be one path;

however, I fear that while currently occupying a position of retreat, the perilous road is long and distant, and as one's own virtue has not yet been established, it will be difficult to advance upward.
Therefore, the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna said:
"There are two paths for seeking the state of *avaivartika*:
first, the path of difficult practice;..."
"Second is the easy path.

As for what is called the difficult path, it means that in an age of the five turbidities, during a time when no Buddha is present, it is difficult to seek the state of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*).
This challenge has many avenues; briefly stated, there are five.
What are they? First, those who outwardly appear virtuous but who disrupt the Dharma of the Bodhisattvas.
Second, the self-benefit of the śrāvaka obstructs great compassion;
third, disregarding evil persons destroys the superior virtues of others;
fourth, causing all humans and devas to fall into inverted views regarding wholesome fruits ruins the brahmacarya of others.
Fifth, there is only one's own power, without the support of another's power.
Such matters as these are encountered at every turn.
For example, walking on land is arduous; therefore, it is called the "difficult path of practice."

What is called the "easy path" refers to relying on the causal conditions of faith in the Buddha, aspiring to be born in the Pure Land, giving rise to the resolve to cultivate virtue, and practicing various meritorious deeds; by the power of the Buddha's vows, one is then immediately reborn there.
Sustained by the Buddha’s power, they immediately enter the stage of the right determination of the Mahāyāna;
this "stage of right determination" refers to the state of non-retrogression, known as *avaivartika*.
For example, it is like traveling by boat on a waterway, which is pleasant; therefore, it is called the "Easy Path.
A question is asked:
"Since Bodhi is one, the cultivation of its causes should likewise be non-dual."

Why is it that practicing the causes for the fruit of Buddhahood here [in this world] is called a "difficult practice," whereas aspiring for great Bodhi through rebirth in a Pure Land is called an "easy path"?
He replied:
"All the dharmas of practice expounded in the Mahāyāna sūtras possess both self-power and other-power, as well as being encompassed by oneself and encompassed by others."
What is self-power?

For example, suppose there is a person who, out of fear of birth and death, resolves to leave the household life, cultivates meditative concentration, and develops supernormal powers, traveling throughout the four continents; this is called self-power.
What is "other-power" (*parakrama*)?

It is like a weak man who, by his own physical strength, is unable to throw a donkey over a wall; yet if he relies upon a Universal Monarch (*cakravartin*), he can immediately travel through the four continents by soaring through the air. This is due to the sovereign power of the Universal Monarch, and is therefore called "other-power."
Sentient beings are likewise: when they give rise to the aspiration and establish the practice here with the vow to be born in the Pure Land, this is their own power (*svabala*);
when, at the time of death, the Tathāgata Amitābha welcomes them upon his radiant platform so that they attain birth there, this is the power of others (*parabala*).
Therefore, the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states:

"Among the humans and devas of the ten directions who wish to be born in my land, there are none who do not take the power of the great vows and karmic deeds of Amitābha Tathāgata as their dominant condition."
"If it were not thus, the forty-eight vows would be established in vain. Speaking to later learners:
since there is the power of others (tariki) upon which one may rely, one must not confine oneself to one's own limited capacity and remain in vain within the burning house."
Second, to clarify the great and small kalpas:
as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states, "There are three kinds of kalpas: [the intermediate, the great, and the small]."
This refers to one small, two medium, and three great [kalpas].
Suppose there is a city forty *li* square, with a height and depth equal to its width, filled to the brim with mustard seeds.
If long-lived devas were to remove one seed every three years until all the mustard seeds were exhausted, this duration is called one small kalpa (*antarakalpa*).

Alternatively, if there is a city eighty *li* in extent, with its height and depth being the same, and it is filled with mustard seeds which are removed one by one until exhausted as previously described, this is called one *antara-kalpa*.

Alternatively, if there is a city one hundred and twenty *li* in extent, with its height and depth being the same, and it is filled with mustard seeds which are removed until exhausted in the same manner as before, only then is it called a *mahā-kalpa*.

There is a stone eighty *li* in size, with its height and depth being the same. There is a certain long-lived deva who, once every three years, brushes it with a celestial robe. This celestial robe weighs only three *zhu*; yet, by brushing it incessantly, this stone is eventually worn away. This period is called an intermediate kalpa (*antarakalpa*).
The small and large stones may be understood through the preceding account of the intermediate kalpas; there is no need to describe them in detail.
Within the third section, there are five parts:
first, it clarifies that since beginningless kalpas, one has wandered endlessly in this saṃsāra, undergoing countless births.
As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"Among human beings, one may die in the Zhang family and be born in the Wang family;
or die in the Wang family and be born in the Li family."
In this manner, throughout the entire realm of Jambudvīpa— whether being reborn in the same family or a different family, or dying in southern Jambudvīpa and being born in western Aparagoyānī—
the same applies to the other three continents as it does to Jambudvīpa.
As it is with those who die in the four continents and are reborn among the Four Great Kings,
so it is with those who die among the Four Great Kings and are reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven;
and as it is with those who die in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and are reborn in the other four higher heavens, so it is likewise.

The realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) consists of eighteen tiers of heavens, and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) consists of four tiers of heavens; dying here and being born there in each and every instance is likewise universal.
Or, one may die in the realm of form and be born in the Avīci Hell;
or die within the Avīci Hell and be born in other minor hells.
Dying in the Hell of Light Bonds, one is reborn among animals;
dying among animals, one is reborn in the realm of hungry ghosts;
dying in the realm of hungry ghosts, one may be reborn among humans or devas.

Thus one wanders through the six realms of saṃsāra, experiencing the two retributions of suffering and pleasure; birth and death are endless. Just as it is with birth from a womb, so it is with the other three modes of birth.
Therefore, the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* states:
"The Bodhisattva, born by transformation, addressed the assembly of devas, saying:

'Ordinary people pass through hundreds of thousands of such births, yet they remain attached to pleasure and negligent, failing to cultivate the Path. Unaware that their past merits have been gradually exhausted, they fall back into the three miserable realms to undergo manifold sufferings.'"
Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
"This body is a collection of suffering; everything about it is impure. It is a yoke, a fetter, an abscess, and a wound—fundamentally devoid of any benefit."
"Up to the bodies of the various devas, it is likewise thus.
Therefore, that sutra further says:
"Exhort the cultivation of heedfulness."
Why is this? For negligence is the root of all evils,
while non-negligence is the source of all virtues.
Just as the light of the sun and moon is the foremost among all forms of illumination,
so too is the dharma of heedfulness the most supreme among all wholesome dharmas.
Just as Sumeru, the King of Mountains, is the most preeminent and supreme among all mountains;
so too is the dharma of heedfulness the most preeminent and supreme among all wholesome dharmas.
Why is this? All unwholesome dharmas arise from heedlessness;
all wholesome dharmas have heedfulness as their root.
Second, he asked:

"Although it is said that since beginningless kalpas the cycle of the six realms has been boundless, we do not yet know how many bodies one undergoes within a single kalpa before speaking of such 'transmigration'."
He replied: "As stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*:

'If one were to take all the grasses and trees of the trichiliocosm and cut them into tally-sticks four inches long to count the number of times one has received a body, a father, and a mother throughout a single kalpa, they would still not be exhausted.'"
Some say: "The milk drunk from one's mother's breast during a single kalpa exceeds the waters of the four great oceans. Others say:
"The bodily bones accumulated within a single kalpa are like Mount Vipula.
Thus, having undergone birth and death for such distant kalpas, one remains a mere ordinary person even unto this day; why have you never reflected upon this, sighing with grief without end?
Third, he asked again:
"Since it is said that throughout vast eons one has received countless bodies, is this intended merely as a general statement to cause people to feel weary [of cyclic existence]?"
"Is there also scriptural evidence to prove this?
He replied,
"All of these are explicit passages from the holy teachings."
Why is this? As stated in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*:
"In the past, incalculably many great kalpas ago, there appeared in the world a Buddha named Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū Tathāgata."
There were sixteen princes, each ascending a Dharma seat to teach and transform sentient beings.
Each and every prince individually taught and transformed six million billion nayutas of sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River.
"Since that Buddha entered parinirvāṇa, an extremely long period of time has passed, such that it cannot even be calculated or known. Why is this?
As the sutra says:
"Suppose one were to take the entire great earth of a trichiliocosm and grind it into ink.
The Buddha said:
'If this person were to drop a single dot, as small as a minute mote of dust, after passing through a thousand lands, and continued in this manner until all the ink from the earth was exhausted.'"
The Buddha said:
"If one were to take all the lands this person has passed through— whether marked or unmarked— and grind them all into dust, with each particle of dust representing one kalpa,
the time since that Buddha entered parinirvāṇa would exceed even that number."
"The sentient beings of today are none other than those sixteen princes who, at that time, received the teachings from beneath my seat.
Therefore, the sutra says:
"On account of these fundamental causes and conditions, I preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* for them."
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* further states:
"One was a prince and the other was a poor man; these two men thus came and went between one another.
As for the one called the prince, he is today the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, who was that sixteenth prince at that time."
"As for those called 'the poor,' they are none other than the sentient beings of today. Fourth, he asked:
"Since these sentient beings have been said to transmigrate through many kalpas, among the three realms, in which destination (gati) do they take birth most frequently?"
He replied:
"Although it is said that one wanders [in saṃsāra], one predominantly receives bodies within the three evil realms.
As it is said in the Sūtra:"
"Within the void of space, measuring eight cubits in circumference and extending from the earth up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven—
within this measured space, all visible sentient beings are more numerous than the bodies of humans and devas in a trichiliocosm."
Thus we know that bodies in the evil realms are numerous. Why is this so?
It is simply because unwholesome states arise easily, whereas a wholesome mind is difficult to produce.
If we examine the sentient beings of the present time, those who attain wealth and status engage solely in indulgence and violate the precepts;
likewise, among the gods, many remain attached to their pleasures.
Therefore, a sutra says:
"Sentient beings alike undergo transmigration, constantly taking the three evil realms as their permanent home;
humans and devas visit only briefly before departing, for which reason they are called mere guest houses."
According to the *Mahālaṃkāra-śāstra*, one should exhort all sentient beings that they must always maintain mindfulness before them. A verse therein says:

"When in the prime of youth and free from affliction, if one is indolent and fails to practice with diligence, busying oneself with various worldly affairs instead of cultivating generosity, ethical discipline, and meditation, then when on the verge of being swallowed by death, one will only then regret not having sought to cultivate goodness."
The wise should observe and sever the perceptions of the five desires; those who diligently train the mind will have no regret at the time of death.
When the mind is focused and free from confused thoughts, the wise apply themselves with diligence, so that their intent remains undistracted at the moment of passing.

If one does not practice with a concentrated mind, it will surely be distracted at the time of death; when the mind is distracted, it is like a horse being broken with a grindstone, or like a soldier in battle who circles about instead of marching straight forward.
Fifth, he asked again:
"If all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature and have encountered many Buddhas throughout distant kalpas,
for what reason do they still wander through birth and death to this day, failing to emerge from the burning house?"
He replied:

"According to the noble teachings of the Mahāyāna, it is precisely because they have not attained two kinds of supreme dharmas that they are unable to cast off birth and death; therefore, they do not emerge from the burning house."
What are these two?
The first is the Noble Path;
the second is rebirth in the Pure Land.
This single path of the sages is difficult to realize in the present age for two reasons:
first, because it is remote from the Great Sage;
and second, because its principles are profound and its explanations subtle.
Therefore, the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-candragarbha-sūtra* states:
"In the age of the Final Dharma, among the hundreds of millions of sentient beings who initiate practice and cultivate the Way, not a single person shall attain it."
"In this present age of the Final Dharma, manifesting as this world of the five turbidities and evil, there is only the single gateway of the Pure Land through which one may gain entry.
Therefore, the *Mahāyāna Sūtra* states:

'If there are sentient beings who, even if they have committed evil throughout their entire lives, should at the moment of death continue ten recitations of my name with uninterrupted mindfulness—if they are not reborn [there], may I not attain perfect enlightenment.'"

"Furthermore, all sentient beings utterly fail to measure themselves. If one considers the Mahāyāna, they have never applied their minds to True Suchness (*tathatā*), the Real Aspect (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), or the Emptiness of the Ultimate Meaning (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).

If one discusses the Hīnayāna, from the cultivation of entry into the vision of the Truth (*darśanamārga*) and the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), up to the stages of Anāgāmin and Arhat—wherein the five lower fetters are severed and the five higher fetters are eliminated—not to mention the distinction between monastics and laypeople, none of them possess such a portion."
Even if there are fruits of rebirth as humans or devas, all such rewards are summoned by the five precepts and the ten wholesome actions; yet those who can maintain them are extremely rare.
As for the arising of evil and the commission of transgressions, how are they different from a violent wind and torrential rain?
For this reason, the Buddhas, out of their great compassion, exhort us to take refuge in the Pure Land.

Even if one has committed evil throughout an entire lifetime, provided they can focus their minds with single-minded devotion and constantly practice mindfulness of the Buddha, all obstacles will naturally be eliminated, and rebirth in that land is certain.
"Why do you not reflect upon this? You have no intention at all to depart.
From here below is the fourth section, which cites sacred teachings to provide proof and encourages those who seek rebirth [in the Pure Land] to have faith.
According to the *Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi-sūtra*:
At that time, in the assembly, the Bodhisattva Dhanapati addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
I recall that in the past, immeasurable kalpas ago, there was a Buddha who appeared in the world, also named Śākyamuni Buddha."
After that Buddha had passed into extinction, there was a prince named Suvarṇadhvaja who was arrogant and held false views, having no faith in the True Dharma.
A learned bhikṣu named Samādhisvatantra addressed the prince, saying:
"In the world there is an image of the Buddha that is exceedingly lovely; you should enter the stūpa for a moment to behold the form of the Buddha."
Then, following the words of his good friend, the prince entered the stūpa to view the image. Seeing the marks and signs of the image, he said:
"Bhikṣu! If the Buddha’s image is already so majestic and dignified, how much more so must the Buddha’s true body be?"
The bhikṣu said: "Prince!
If you see a Buddha image now and are unable to prostrate, you should simply recite 'Namo Buddhāya'."

Returning to the palace, he focused his mind on the image within the stūpa; then, during the final watch of the night, he saw the Buddha’s image in a dream. His heart was filled with great joy, and he abandoned his wrong views, taking refuge in the Triple Gem.
At the end of his life, by virtue of having previously entered a stupa and recited the merits of the Buddha, he immediately encountered nine hundred billion nayutas of Buddhas.
In the presence of these Buddhas, he was always diligent and energetic, constantly attaining the profound *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*.

By the power of the *nien-fo* samādhi, all Buddhas appeared before him and bestowed upon him predictions of enlightenment; from that time until today, throughout ten million *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, he has not fallen into the evil realms, and has now attained the Śūraṅgama Samādhi.
"The prince at that time was none other than I, Dhanapati, here and now.

At that moment, there were immeasurable great bodhisattvas from the ten directions within the assembly, each recounting their own past causes and conditions, all of which had been attained through mindfulness of the Buddha.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"This Samādhi of Contemplating the Buddha is the medicine for all sentient beings who have committed offenses; it is the protection for those who have broken the precepts, the guide for those who have lost the Way, the eyes for those in blind darkness, and the wisdom for those who are ignorant. It is a lamp for those in the gloom, a most valiant general amidst the thieves of affliction, the playground of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, and the primary place of origin for the great samādhis such as Śūraṅgama."
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"You must now uphold this well; be careful not to forget or lose it.
All Buddhas of the three periods—past, future, and present—have all taught this very same Buddha-remembrance samādhi."

I, together with the Buddhas of the ten directions and the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa, have all attained the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā) from our first generation of the mind of awakening, solely through the power of the samādhi of mindfulness of the Buddha.
Furthermore, as stated in the *Maudgalyāyana-paripṛcchā-sūtra*:
“The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:

‘It is like the vast currents of ten thousand rivers; upon them float grasses and trees that do not look back to what is behind nor look forward to what is ahead, yet they all converge in the great ocean.’”
The world is likewise: though one may possess nobility, wealth, pleasure, and mastery, none can escape birth, old age, sickness, and death.

It is solely because of a lack of faith in the Buddhist scriptures that, in future lives as humans, one will suffer even greater hardship and distress, and be unable to be born in the lands of the thousand Buddhas.

For this reason, I say that the land of the Buddha Amitāyus is easy to reach and easy to attain; yet people are unable to practice for rebirth there, instead serving the ninety-five kinds of heterodox paths. I declare that such people are called those without eyes and those without ears.
"Since the scriptural teachings are thus, why not abandon the difficult path and rely instead on the easy practice?
