Compiled by Shi Daochuo,
the fourth major section contains three points of analysis: First, based on the Chinese Tripiṭaka Master as well as the great virtuous ones of this land,
all of whom have thoroughly examined the sacred teachings and praised their return to the Pure Land, I now exhort you to rely upon them.

Second, according to the tenets of this sutra and other Mahayana schools, the cultivation and entry of both ordinary beings and sages primarily clarify the *nien-fo samādhi* (Buddha-recollection samādhi) as the essential gateway;
third, through the questions and answers, it is revealed that those who practice Buddha-recollection attain various functional benefits that are inconceivable.
First, regarding the practices followed by the great masters of China and this land:
as for the remaining five [treatises] that obscure the face like a wall, how could I presume to act on my own?
I have merely traveled to investigate and examine them, respectfully acknowledging their lineage of transmission.
Who were they? They were the Mahāyāna Dharma Master Paramārtha, the Tripiṭaka Master from Central India;
next was the Venerable Huìpǐng, who shunned fame and profit; and then there was the Dharma Master Huìcóng.
Next was a virtuous elder who regularly expounded the Dharma; whenever he felt the Holy Sangha come to listen, there appeared the Dharma Master Daochang.
Next was a virtuous elder who lived in solitary seclusion while blending with the common world, whom both countries admired and looked up to; this was the Dharma Master Tanyuan.
Next was a virtuous elder whose meditative contemplation stood out uniquely; this was the Chan Master Dahan.
Next was a virtuous elder, wise and observant of the precepts, who served as the Superior Administrator of the Qi court.

Indeed, these six preceding great elders were all like divine mirrors reflecting the Two Truths; they were the pillars of the Buddha-dharma, whose aspirations and conduct were peerless, truly rare throughout both past and present.
Together they examined the Mahāyāna in detail and praised their taking refuge in the Pure Land, saying that this is indeed the unsurpassed essential gate.
Someone asked:
"Since it is said that praising and taking refuge in the Pure Land is the essential gate, I wonder whether these virtuous masters all experienced spiritual efficacy at the time of their death?"
He replied: "All of them are indeed not in vain.
For instance, while the Dharma Master Tanluan was still alive, he constantly cultivated the Pure Land; yet there were often worldly gentlemen who came to rebuke the Master, saying:"
"The Buddha-lands of the ten directions are all pure lands; why then do you, O Dharma Master, single-mindedly fix your intent upon the West?
Is this not the arising of a biased view?
The Dharma Master replied:
"I am but an ordinary person, my wisdom shallow and limited, and I have not yet entered the stages of realization; therefore, my power of mindfulness must be balanced.
It is like tethering a cow with straw—my mind must always be bound to the manger."
"How can they be left to roam at will, with no place of refuge at all?
Although the objectors were numerous and their arguments manifold, the Dharma Master alone resolved them.
Therefore, whether among the clergy or the laity, anyone who encountered the Dharma Master even once—if they had not yet developed right faith—was exhorted by him to do so.
If there are those who have already developed right faith, they should all be exhorted to return to the Pure Land.

Therefore, when the Dharma Master approaches the end of his life, the monastics and laypeople nearby on all sides shall see banners and flowers reflecting in the courtyard, everyone will perceive a wondrous fragrance, and music will welcome him as he attains rebirth there.
"The other great virtuous ones all exhibited auspicious signs at the time of their passing; if one were to recount in detail the manifestations of their rebirths, they would all be inconceivable.
Second, it clarifies that among the various sutras, many take the *nien-fo san-mei* (Buddha-recollection samādhi) as their primary tenet.
Within this, there are eight sections:

the first two clarify the samādhi of one characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇa-samādhi*), while the subsequent six clarify the *nien-fo* (Buddha-recollection) samādhi in relation to conditions and based on characteristics.
First, according to the *Puṣpasūtra*:
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Resolute Mind:
“There are two kinds of samādhi:
first, there is the samādhi of a single characteristic;”
Second, there is the samādhi of various marks (*nānā-lakṣaṇa-samādhi*).

Regarding the samādhi of a single mark (*eka-lakṣaṇa-samādhi*): there are bodhisattvas who, having heard that a Tathāgata currently exists and is preaching the Dharma in a certain world, take up the marks of that Buddha so that he appears before them—whether sitting at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) or turning the wheel of the Dharma, surrounded by a great assembly.
Grasping such signs, he withdraws his sense faculties so that the mind does not wander; he focuses single-mindedly on one Buddha and does not abandon this object of focus.

Thus, the Bodhisattva thoroughly understands that the marks of the Tathāgata and the marks of the world are signless; he constantly contemplates in this way and practices in this way, never departing from this object of focus.
At that time, the image of the Buddha appeared before him and preached the Dharma for him.
The Bodhisattva then gave rise to profound reverence and listened to and received this teaching; whether it was profound or shallow, his respect increased all the more.

When a bodhisattva dwells in this samādhi, they hear it taught that all dharmas possess the characteristic of being subject to disintegration; having heard this, they receive and uphold it, and upon arising from the samādhi, they are able to expound this dharma for the fourfold assembly.
The Buddha told Resolute Mind:
“This is called the bodhisattva’s entry into the samādhi-gate of the single characteristic.
Second, regarding the elucidation of the *ekavyūha-samādhi* according to the *Mañjuśrī-prajñā*:
At that time, Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what is meant by the ‘samādhi of a single practice’?”
The Buddha said:

"As for the Samādhi of One Practice, if a good man or a good woman should dwell in a secluded place, abandon all distracted thoughts, and face the direction where the Buddha resides with body upright and mind directed forward; without grasping at physical appearances, they should fix their minds on a single Buddha, single-mindedly reciting that name, maintaining mindfulness without rest."
This is because within that very mindfulness, one is able to see the Buddhas of the three periods—past, present, and future.
Why is this? Because the merit of one Buddha is immeasurable and boundless; it is non-dual from the merit of immeasurable Buddhas. This is called the Bodhisattva’s Samādhi of One Practice.
Third, according to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*:
"The Buddha said:

'If a person can simply cultivate the samādhi of mindfulness of the Buddha with a sincere heart at all times, the Buddhas of the ten directions will constantly behold this person as if they were standing before them.'"
Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Kāśyapa:

'If there are sons of good family or daughters of good family who are always able to mindfully recollect the Buddha with a sincere heart—whether in mountain forests or in villages, whether by day or by night, whether sitting or lying down—the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, will constantly see these people as if they were right before their eyes.'"
"I shall always dwell with this person and accept their offerings.

Fourth, according to the *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra* and other various sections, regarding the myriad practices one cultivates, if one can simply dedicate and vow them [toward rebirth], there are none that will not lead to birth [in the Pure Land].
Nevertheless, the single practice of mindfulness of the Buddha shall serve as the essential path. Why is this?
Upon careful examination of the sacred teachings, they provide benefit at both the beginning and the end.
If one wishes to give rise to wholesome states and initiate practice, then one universally encompasses all the perfections (pāramitās);
if one seeks to extinguish evil and eliminate calamities, then one comprehensively remedies all obstacles.
Therefore, the subsequent scripture says:
"The sentient beings who practice mindfulness of the Buddha are gathered and not abandoned.
At the end of their lives, they will certainly be born [in the Pure Land]; this is called the "initial benefit.
Regarding the "ultimate benefit," according to the *Avalokiteśvara-vyākaraṇa-sūtra*, it says:
"Amitābha Buddha remains in the world for a long duration; even after ten billion eons, he shall enter parinirvāṇa.
At the time of his parinirvāṇa, only Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta shall remain to sustain the Land of Peace and Bliss, guiding and receiving beings from the ten directions."
The duration of that Buddha’s parinirvāṇa is equal to the length of time he remained in the world.

Nevertheless, among the sentient beings of that land, there are none who behold the Buddha, except for those who single-mindedly and exclusively contemplate Amitābha Buddha and attain rebirth there; these individuals constantly see Amitābha, who remains present and does not pass away.
"This is precisely the benefit at the time of his passing.
All other practices he cultivated were dedicated toward rebirth.
Whether the World-Honored One was seen or not seen after his parinirvāṇa, he exhorted future generations to deliberate with discernment, so that they might partake in this far-reaching benefit."
Fifth, according to the *Pratyutpanna-samādhi Sūtra*:
"At that time, there was a bodhisattva named Bhadrapāla who, in this land, heard of the existence of Amitābha Buddha and repeatedly focused his mindfulness upon him."
Because of this thought, he beheld Amitābha Buddha.
Having seen the Buddha, he immediately addressed him with a question:
"By practicing what Dharma may one attain birth in that land?"
At that time, Amitābha Buddha spoke to these bodhisattvas, saying:
"Those who wish to come and be born in my land must constantly recollect my name without ceasing; in this way, they shall succeed in being born in my buddha-field."
"One should contemplate the Buddha’s body as being fully endowed with the thirty-two marks, its radiance penetrating everywhere, and its form being incomparably upright and handsome.
Sixth, according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, there are three successive explanations.

First, the Buddha is the unsurpassed Dharma King and the Bodhisattvas are his Dharma ministers; that which they revere and honor is solely the World-Honored Buddha, and for this reason, one should constantly practice the recollection of the Buddha.
Second, there are Bodhisattvas who say of themselves:

"Since the beginningless kalpas, we have been nurtured by the World-Honored One with our Dharma-body, Wisdom-body, and Great Compassion-body; our meditative concentration, wisdom, and immeasurable practices and vows were accomplished through the Buddha."
"To repay their gratitude, they always vow to remain near the Buddha;
it is just as a high minister who, having received the sovereign's favor and grace, constantly keeps his lord in mind.
Third, there are other bodhisattvas who further speak thus:
"In my stage as a bodhisattva, I encountered evil associates who slandered the Prajñāpāramitā; consequently, I fell into the evil realms and remained there for immeasurable kalpas.
Although I practiced other paths, I was unable to escape."

Later, at one time, under the guidance of a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), he was taught the practice of the Buddha-recollection samādhi (buddhānusmṛti-samādhi); at that moment, he was able to simultaneously dispel all obstacles and finally attained liberation.
Because there is such great benefit, I vow never to be separated from the Buddha.
Seventh, according to the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*:
"I would rather undergo all manner of suffering throughout immeasurable kalpas than ever distance myself from the Tathāgata or fail to behold his sovereign power."
It further states:

"Through the samādhi of mindfulness of the Buddha, one will certainly see the Buddha; after the end of life, one will be reborn before the Buddha. Seeing others at the point of death, one encourages them to practice mindfulness of the Buddha, and furthermore displays a sacred image for them to behold with reverence."
Furthermore, the youth Sudhana, seeking spiritual friends, went to the bhikṣu Guṇamegha and said to him:
"Great Teacher!
How does one cultivate the bodhisattva path so as to return to the conduct of Samantabhadra?"
At that time, the bhikṣu said to Sudhana:
"Within the ocean of the World-Honored One’s wisdom, I know but a single dharma, namely, the gate of the samādhi of mindfulness of the Buddha."

Why is this? Within this gate of samādhi, one is able to behold all Buddhas and their retinues, as well as the adorned and purified Buddha-fields, and can cause sentient beings to distance themselves from inverted views.
The gate of the Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha is to perceive the sovereign realm of all Buddhas within subtle objects, thereby attaining non-delusion regarding all kalpas;

the gate of the Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha is able to manifest all Buddha-lands such that none can destroy them, universally beholding all Buddhas and attaining non-delusion regarding the three periods of time.
Then the bhikṣu Guṇamegha said to Sudhana:

"The ocean of the Buddha-dharma is deep, vast, and boundless. Of that which I know, I have only attained this single gate of the *ekakṣaṇa-smṛti-samādhi*; as for other wondrous realms that transcend all measure and number, they are unknown to me."
Eighth, according to the *Sāgaranāgarājaparipṛcchā-sūtra*:
"At that time, the Dragon King Sāgara addressed the Buddha, saying:
'World-Honored One!'"
“Disciple, if one seeks birth in the land of Amitābha Buddha, what practices should one cultivate to attain rebirth in that realm?
The Buddha told the Dragon King:
“If you wish to be born in that land, you should practice eight dharmas.”
What are the eight?
First, constantly recollecting all Buddhas;
second, making offerings to the Tathāgatas.
Third, to praise and extol the World-Honored One;
fourth, to fashion images of the Buddha and cultivate all manner of meritorious virtues;
fifth, to dedicate these merits with the vow to be reborn [in that land].
Sixth, the mind is not timid or weak;
seventh, single-minded diligence;
eighth, seeking the Buddha’s true wisdom.
The Buddha told the Dragon King:
"All sentient beings who possess these eight qualities are never separated from the Buddha. He asked:
“Without possessing these eight qualities, can one be born before the Buddha and never be separated from him?
He replied, “One will be born there; of this there is no doubt.”
How is this known?
It is as the Buddha taught in the *Ratnamegha Sūtra*: when one fully accomplishes the ten practices, one will be born in the Pure Land and never be separated from the Buddha.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Is it possible to be reborn there even without possessing the ten practices?
The Buddha said:
"You shall attain rebirth.
However, if among these ten practices one is fully perfected without deficiency, the remaining nine practices are all termed "pure.
Do not harbor any doubts.
Furthermore, the *Mahādruma-kinnara-rāja-paripṛcchā-sūtra* states:
"If a bodhisattva practices four kinds of dharmas, they will never be separated from the presence of the Buddha.
What are these four?"
First, to personally cultivate wholesome dharmas while simultaneously exhorting sentient beings to all aspire for rebirth there, thereby perceiving the intention of the Tathāgata;
second, to personally exhort and encourage others to delight in hearing the True Dharma;
third, to personally exhort and encourage others to resolve upon Bodhicitta.
"Fourth, to single-mindedly and exclusively practice the *nien-fo* samādhi.
One who possesses these four practices will always be in the presence of the Buddhas in all places of birth, never being separated from them."
Furthermore, a sutra states:
"The Buddha taught that there are thirty-two vessels for the practices of a bodhisattva. What are they?"

Generosity is the vessel for great wealth; patience is the vessel for physical beauty; upholding the precepts is the vessel for a noble body; the five heinous crimes and filial impiety are the vessels for the mountain of knives, the forest of swords, and the cauldron of boiling water; the arousal of the bodhicitta is the vessel for attaining Buddhahood; and the constant practice of mindfulness of the Buddha to be reborn in the Pure Land is the vessel for beholding the Buddha.
Thus, six categories have been briefly cited, while the remainder are not described.
Since the holy teachings are thus, why should a practitioner who aspires for rebirth there not constantly practice mindfulness of the Buddha?
Furthermore, according to the *Samādhirāja Sūtra*:

"By recollecting the Buddha’s physical marks and excellence, as well as his virtuous conduct, one can cause the sense faculties to remain undisturbed; with a mind free from delusion, one accords with the Dharma, attaining hearing and wisdom like a great ocean."

The wise one dwelling in this samādhi, with mindfulness gathered while walking in the place of *caṅkrama*, is able to see billions of Tathāgatas and also encounter Buddhas as numerous as the sands of immeasurable Ganges Rivers.
Third, the question-and-answer explanation reveals that the *nien-fo san-mei* (Buddha-recollection samādhi) possesses various benefits.
It consists of five sections.
First, the question is as follows:
"Now you say that one should constantly practice the *nien-fo san-mei* (Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi), yet still not practice other samādhis?
He replied:

"What I mean by 'constant mindfulness' does not imply that one does not practice other samādhis; rather, because the practice of the *nien-fo san-mei* is predominant, it is called 'constant mindfulness,' not to suggest that one entirely refrains from practicing other samādhis."
Second, the question was asked:
"If one encourages the constant cultivation of the *nien-fo* samādhi (Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi), is there a distinction in degree between it and other samādhis?
The answer was given:
"The supreme characteristics of the Buddha-remembrance samādhi (nienfo sanmei) are inconceivable;
how is this to be known? As it is said in the Mahāyāna:
'All other samādhis are not non-samādhis.'"
Why is this? There are samādhis that can eliminate only greed but cannot eliminate hatred or delusion;
there are samādhis that can eliminate only hatred but cannot eliminate delusion or greed.
There are samādhis that can only eliminate delusion, but cannot eliminate greed and hatred;
there are samādhis that can only eliminate obstacles of the present, but cannot eliminate all obstacles of the past and future.

"If one can constantly cultivate the Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha, then regardless of whether they pertain to the present, past, or future, all obstacles will be entirely eliminated. Third, he asked:

"If the Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha can indeed eliminate obstacles and bring about such great merit and benefit, I wonder if it can also assist the practitioner by causing them to prolong their years and increase their lifespan?"
He replied: "I shall certainly attain it! Why is this?"
As stated in the *Vimokṣa-samādhi Sūtra*:
"There were two brothers; the elder brother believed in cause and effect, while the younger brother lacked faith, yet was skilled in interpreting the marks of physiognomy."
Because he saw within the mirror that the signs of death had already appeared upon his face and would occur no later than seven days hence,
a wise person at that time instructed him to go and question the Buddha.
The Buddha then replied:
"It will not be in vain for seven days.
If you can single-mindedly recite the Buddha’s name and cultivate the precepts, you may attain deliverance from this peril.

Thereupon, he followed these instructions and focused his mind on the Buddha. When the sixth day arrived, two ghosts came; hearing the sound of his recitation of the Buddha's name, they were unable to advance at all and returned to inform King Yama.

In the *Yanluo Wang Suofu* (The Talisman Sought by King Yama), it is already noted that through the merit of observing the precepts and reciting the Buddha’s name, one is reborn in the third heaven, the Yāma Heaven.
Furthermore, in the *Piyu Jing* (Sutra of Parables), there was an elder who did not believe in the retribution of sin and merit; he had already reached the age of fifty.
Suddenly, he dreamed at night that a *kṣetrapāla* spirit had come seeking a talisman to seize him, and that no more than ten days remained.
Upon waking from his sleep, the man was overcome with extraordinary terror.
When morning came, he sought out a physiognomist to interpret his dream; the master cast a divination and declared:
“There is a yakṣa who intends to harm you; it will not exceed ten days.
The man was filled with fear exceeding his usual state and went to the Buddha to seek protection.
The Buddha then replied:

"If you wish to ward this off, from this day forward, you must focus your mind on the Buddha, uphold the precepts, burn incense, light lamps, hang silk banners and canopies, and place your faith in the Triple Gem; thus you may avoid this death."
He then relied upon this Dharma with single-minded faith and devotion.
When the yakṣa arrived at his door, he saw the merit being cultivated and was thus unable to cause harm; the yakṣa immediately fled away.
By virtue of this merit, that person lived out a full hundred years and, upon death, was reborn in heaven.
Furthermore, there was another elder named Dhāraṇa who, having lapsed from his precepts, returned to the Buddha; he was currently being beaten by an evil spirit.
Fourth, he asked:
"Can this Buddha-remembrance samādhi (buddhānusmṛti-samādhi) not only counteract various obstacles and bring about worldly rewards, but also remotely induce supramundane, unsurpassed bodhi?"
He replied: “I have! Which ones?”
As it is said in the "Ten Stages Chapter" of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*:
"From the first stage up to the tenth stage, within each and every stage, the path of application for entering that stage is explained."
Having fulfilled the merits and benefits of the stages, they do not abide until the completion of the path; thus, it is concluded:

"Although these bodhisattvas cultivate other practices, they never depart from mindfulness of the Buddha, mindfulness of the Dharma, and mindfulness of the Sangha, making offerings of supreme and exquisite requisites to the Triple Gem."

Based on this scriptural testimony, one knows that bodhisattvas, up through the higher stages, must constantly practice mindfulness of the Buddha, mindfulness of the Dharma, and mindfulness of the Saṃgha; only then can they fulfill their immeasurable vows and practices and complete the ocean of merit.
How much more so for those of the two vehicles and ordinary beings who seek birth in the Pure Land—how could they not study the practice of Buddha-recollection? Why is this?

Because this samādhi of Buddha-recollection inherently encompasses all four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*) and six perfections (*pāramitā*), serving as both the universal path and its universal companions.
Fifth, it is asked:

"Since Bodhisattvas from the first stage (*bhūmi*) upward have realized the principle of *tathatā* (suchness) in common with the Buddhas and are thus said to be born into the Buddha-family, being able to become Buddhas themselves and deliver sentient beings, why is it necessary for them to further study the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi* (samādhi of mindfulness of the Buddha) and aspire to see the Buddha?"
He replied:
"If one discusses True Suchness (tathatā), it is vast and boundless, equal to space, and its measure is difficult to know.
It is like a large, dark room: even if one lamp or two lamps are lit, although their light pervades the space, it remains dark."
Gradually reaching many lamps, although they are called "great illumination," how could they compare to the light of the sun?
Although the wisdom realized by Bodhisattvas has its own gradations when compared stage by stage, how could it be equated with the Buddha’s wisdom, which is like the brilliance of the sun?
Within the fifth major section, there are four points of analysis:
first, a general clarification regarding the lengthening or shortening of the path of cultivation, intended to enable the swift attainment of non-retrogression;
second, a comparative evaluation of this and that meditative contemplation, exhorting one to proceed [to the former].
Third, the two objects of purity and impurity here and there are also termed the comparison between the outflowing (*sāsrava*) and the outflow-free (*anāsrava*);
fourth, by citing scriptural authority to establish the proof, one exhorts future generations to seek it with faith.

First, a general clarification of the lengthening and shortening of the path of cultivation. Within this, there are two parts: first, clarifying the lengthening and shortening of the path of cultivation; second, [clarifying the lengthening and shortening of the stages].
Regarding the first: clarifying the lengthening and shortening of the path of cultivation.
II. Explanation through Question and Answer.
A. Clarifying Lengthening and Shortening.

All sentient beings without exception loathe suffering and seek happiness; they fear bondage and seek liberation, desiring all to quickly realize unsurpassed bodhi. To this end, one must first take the arousal of the bodhicitta as the primary requirement.
This mind is difficult to recognize and difficult to arouse; even if one succeeds in generating this mind, one must, according to the sūtras, ultimately cultivate ten kinds of practices:

namely, faith, diligence, mindfulness, ethical discipline, meditative concentration, wisdom, equanimity, protection of the Dharma, making vows, and dedication of merit, thereby proceeding toward Bodhi.

However, for one whose body is on the path of cultivation, the succession of moments continues without interruption; only after ten thousand kalpas does one first realize the stage of non-retrogression. At present, ordinary beings are manifestly designated as those with "faith and thought" and "light hair," also called "provisional names," or "the indeterminate group," or "outer ordinary beings"; they have not yet emerged from the burning house.
How is this known?
According to the *Bodhisattva-ālaṃkāra-sūtra*, it is established that the stages of practice for entering the Way are inherently difficult; therefore, it is called the "Difficult Path.

Furthermore, if one cannot even count the number of times one undergoes birth and death within a single kalpa, how much more so the pointlessness of undergoing excruciating torment for ten thousand kalpas?

If one can clearly believe in the Buddha’s sutras and vow to be born in the Pure Land, then regardless of whether their lifespan is long or short, they will reach that land upon the completion of this single lifetime and attain the stage of non-retrogression; this is equal in merit to practicing the Way for ten thousand kalpas.
O Sons of the Buddha!
Why do you not reflect upon this?
Is it not easier to abandon what is difficult to seek than to seek what is difficult to abandon?
As explained in the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, there are two types of paths: the difficult practice and the easy practice. Regarding the difficult practice, the treatise states:

"Throughout three great asaṃkhyeya kalpas, in each and every kalpa, one must complete the provisions of merit and wisdom, as well as all practices of the six pāramitās. Each individual practice contains a million difficult paths; only when these are fulfilled does one attain a single stage. This is the path of difficult practice."
Regarding the "easy path," that same treatise states:
"If there is liberation by means of another expedient, it is called the easy path."

Now, since we have already been exhorted to return to Sukhāvatī, one should dedicate all karmic practices toward that land; provided one can simply be single-mindedly devoted, one will certainly be reborn there at the end of one's life.
Once reborn in that land, one immediately attains ultimate coolness—how could this not be called the path of easy practice?
One must understand this meaning.
Second, a question is asked:

"If it is said that one who vows to be reborn in the Pure Land shall attain rebirth immediately upon the exhaustion of this life, [then what of those who do not die at the end of their natural lifespan?]"
"Is there scriptural authority for this? He replied,
"There are seven sections, all of which cite sūtras and śāstras to establish the proof."
First, according to the *Mahā-sūtra*, it says:
"The Buddha told Ānanda:

'If there are sentient beings who wish to see the Buddha Amitāyus in this very life, they should resolve upon the unsurpassed mind of bodhi, cultivate meritorious virtues, and vow to be born in that land; they shall then attain rebirth there.'"
Thus, the *Mahāvaipulya-sūtra-stotra* says:

"If one hears the name of Amitābha’s virtues and, with a heart of joyful praise and devotion, takes refuge—even for a single thought-moment—one attains great benefit and becomes fully endowed with the treasure of merit."

Even if the great trichiliocosm were filled with fire, one should pass straight through it to hear the Buddha’s name; having heard Amitābha’s name, one shall no longer fall back. For this reason, I bow my head in wholehearted prostration.
2. According to the *Contemplation Sūtra*, it is stated within all nine grades that "if one maintains right mindfulness at the time of death, one will immediately attain rebirth.
3. According to the *Treatise on the Awakening of Faith*, it says:
"I teach all sentient beings to exhort them to contemplate True Suchness as equal, singular, and real.

There are also bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds, whose hearts are weak, and who think to themselves that they cannot constantly encounter the Buddhas to personally receive and make offerings to them, and thus intend to retreat."

One should know that the Tathāgata possesses a supreme skillful means to gather and protect those with faith; namely, through the causal condition of single-minded mindfulness of the Buddha, one is reborn according to one's vow.
Because one constantly beholds the Buddha, one is forever freed from the evil realms.
4. According to the *Dhāraṇī-sūtra of the Drum Sound*, it says:
"At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
'I shall now expound for you concerning the Land of Peace and Bliss in the western direction, where there currently resides a Buddha named Amitābha.'"

If there are members of the fourfold assembly who can correctly receive and uphold the name of that Buddha, firming their resolve and recollecting it without forgetfulness, setting aside all distraction for ten days and ten nights, and diligently practicing the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi* such that the mindfulness is continuous from moment to moment, they will certainly behold that Amitābha Buddha within those ten days and shall all attain rebirth in his land.
5. According to the *Dharmabherī-sūtra*:

"If, at the time of death, a person is unable to form a focused thought, but simply knows that there is a Buddha in that direction and forms the intention to go there, they shall likewise attain rebirth."
6. As stated in the *Sūtra on Rebirth According to One’s Vows in the Ten Directions*:

"If there are those who are at the point of death or have already died and fallen into hell, and their family members and relatives perform the practice of reciting the Buddha's name and chanting scriptures, as well as offering vegetarian feasts and merit for the deceased, the deceased will immediately emerge from hell and attain rebirth in the Pure Land."
How much more so for those who, being currently alive, can personally cultivate mindfulness—how could they fail to attain rebirth there?
Therefore, that sutra says:
"When living relatives perform merit on behalf of the deceased, it is like sending provisions to someone traveling afar; they will certainly receive them."
Seventh, the proof is established by extensively citing various sutras, as stated in the *Mahābherī-haraka-sūtra*:

"If a good man or a good woman is constantly able to fix their mind and recite the names of the Buddhas, all the Buddhas of the ten directions and all the worthy sages will always see this person as if they were right before their eyes."
"For this reason, this sutra is titled 'The Great Dharma Drum. One should know that such a person will be reborn in the pure lands of the ten directions according to their vows.
Furthermore, the *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra* says:
"What is meant by 'great compassion'?"
If one focuses exclusively on the mindfulness of the Buddha with uninterrupted continuity, at the end of life, one will certainly be reborn in peace and bliss.
If one can successively exhort others to practice the mindfulness of the Buddha, it should be known that such persons are all practitioners of great compassion.
Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"The Buddha told the Great King:

'Suppose one were to open a great treasury and bestow its contents upon all sentient beings for the space of one month; the merit thereby obtained would not equal that of a person who utters the name of the Buddha but once. The latter's merit surpasses the former beyond measure.'"
Furthermore, the *Ekottarika Āgama* states:
"The Buddha told Ānanda:
'If there were sentient beings who provided clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicinal requisites to all the people of a single Jambudvīpa, would the merit obtained thereby not be great?'"
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
It is very much so, it is very much so!”
"It is immeasurable.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"If there are sentient beings who, with a continuous virtuous mind, recite the name of the Buddha for as long as it takes to milk a cow once, the merit they obtain will surpass the aforementioned and be immeasurable; no one can measure it."
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:
"If a person recollects the Buddha with a distracted mind, their merit shall not be exhausted until they have reached the end of suffering;
if a person recollects the Buddha by scattering flowers, their merit shall not be exhausted until they have reached the end of suffering."
Thus we know that the benefit of mindfulness of the Buddha is great and inconceivable.
There are textual proofs for this in the *Sūtra on the Ten Ways of Rebirth* and various other Mahāyāna sūtras, though they cannot be cited in full here.
Second, next is the clarification of a comparison between this and that meditative contemplation (*dhyāna*), exhorting those who would seek rebirth therein.

However, this world is a defiled realm where distracted thoughts make entry difficult; even if one succeeds in cultivation, one attains only mundane concentration (*samādhi*) and mostly delights in the defilement of its flavors.
Furthermore, those who merely suppress their karma may be reborn in the higher realms, yet when their lifespan ends, they mostly fall back.
Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:

"Though one possesses much learning, maintains the precepts, and practices dhyāna, if one has not yet attained the untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*), these merits, though present, cannot yet be relied upon."

If one wishes to practice facing west, the objective realm will become luminous and pure; meditative observation will easily be accomplished, sins from many kalpas will be eliminated, and one will certainly and swiftly advance toward ultimate coolness.
As explained at length in the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*. Question:

"If the realms of the western direction are superior and can be induced by meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), why should this realm of the Form Heavens (*rūpabhava*)—being inferior—not be summoned by meditative concentration?"
He replied:
"If one discusses the causes for cultivating meditative concentration, they apply universally to both that [realm] and this one.
However, because that realm is a stage of non-retrogression and is sustained by the power of others, it is said to be superior."

Although one may cultivate meditative concentration here with diligence, there exists only the internal cause (svabhāva-hetu) and lacks the encompassing power of another; thus, when karma is exhausted, one cannot avoid falling back. In this regard, it is said that this state is inferior.
Third, regarding these two objects—the pure and the defiled—they are also termed "outflowing" (*sāsrava*) and "non-outflowing" (*anāsrava*).

If one discusses the objects of this realm, there are only the three miserable paths, mounds and pits, mountain ravines, saline wastelands, thorns, floods and droughts, violent winds and harsh touches, thunder, lightning, and hail, tigers, wolves, and venomous beasts, wicked robbers and evil children, desolation and ruin, and destruction by the three calamities.

To speak of their primary retributions: the three poisons, the eight inversions, sorrow, grief, jealousy, and envy; much illness and short lifespans; hunger, thirst, cold, and heat; and being constantly pursued by the spirits of death and harm. These are profoundly loathsome and cannot be fully described; therefore, they are called "outflowing" and are deeply to be reviled.

Regarding those who are superior in being reborn in that land, according to the *Mahāyāna Sūtra*, among the humans and devas of the ten directions who are born there, there are none who do not obtain various kinds of benefits.

What are these? First, those born in that land: when walking, golden lotuses support their feet; when sitting, precious thrones sustain their bodies; when going out, Śakra stands before them; when entering, Brahmā follows behind them;
all the holy assembly are their kinsmen and friends, and Amitābha Buddha is their Great Teacher.
They soar at will beneath jeweled trees and gemstone groves; they sport their spirits and bathe their feet in ponds of the eight virtues.
Their forms are identical to golden hue, and their lifespans are equal to those of the Buddhas.
In study, they advance through all gateways simultaneously; in cessation, the two truths merge into emptiness.

When delivering and transporting beings throughout the ten directions, one rides upon great supernormal powers (*abhijñā*); when resting in peace for a time, one sits within the three gates of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
When wandering, one enters the path of the Eightfold Noble Path; when arriving, one reaches Great Nirvāṇa (*mahānirvāṇa*).
All sentient beings who merely reach that land shall realize these benefits; why then do you not reflect upon this and go there with haste?
Fourth, citing the sacred teachings to provide proof, I exhort those of future generations to give rise to faith and aspire to go there.
According to the *Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi-sūtra*:
"At that time, Buddhas from the ten directions appeared in the sky, each sitting cross-legged upon a lotus pedestal within the assembly."
The Tathāgata Śubhavyūha of the eastern quarter addressed the great assembly, saying:
"You should know this!
I recall that in the past, immeasurable eons ago, there was a Buddha named Ratnatejobhyudgatarāja."
When that Buddha appeared in the world, he also preached the Dharma of the Three Vehicles just as I do today.
After that Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, during the final age, there was a bhikṣu who, accompanied by nine disciples, went to a Buddhist stūpa to pay homage to the Buddha’s image.

They saw a precious image, magnificent and beautiful to behold; having seen it, they paid homage and gazed upon it with fixed attention, each reciting a verse as a hymn of praise, and then they passed away according to the length of their respective lifespans.

Immediately after his life ended, he was reborn before the Buddha; from that time forth, he constantly encountered immeasurable Buddhas, and in the presence of those Buddhas, he extensively cultivated pure conduct and attained the ocean-like samādhi of mindfulness of the Buddha.
Having attained this, the Buddhas appeared before him and immediately bestowed upon him the prediction that he would become a Buddha according to his wish in the ten directions.
The Buddha of Good Virtue in the eastern direction is none other than my own self;
as for the Buddhas in the remaining nine directions, they are the nine disciples from my past lives.
The Buddhas of the ten directions, the World-Honored Ones, attained Buddhahood because they offered a single verse of praise while circumambulating a stupa; could they have been anyone else?
We, the Buddhas of the ten directions, are they.

At that time, the Buddhas of the ten directions descended from the sky, emitting a thousand rays of light and manifesting their physical bodies; the radiance from the white tufts between their brows shone forth as each sat upon the seat of Śākyamuni Buddha and addressed Ānanda, saying:
"You should know that Śākyamuni Buddha, through countless efforts and hundreds of thousands of ascetic practices, sought the wisdom of a Buddha and attained this body as its retribution."

I shall now speak for you; uphold these words of the Buddha and, for the sake of the great assemblies of devas and nāgas and the fourfold assembly of disciples in future ages, teach them the contemplation of the Buddha’s marks and signs and the samādhi of mindfulness of the Buddha.
Having spoken these words, they then paid their respects to Śākyamuni Buddha; once their greetings were concluded, each returned to his own land.
Within this sixth major section, there are three sections of analysis:
first, the mutual comparison of the pure lands of the ten directions.
Second, the inference based on meaning;
third, the analysis of the sūtra’s abiding and cessation.
First, regarding the comparison of the pure lands of the ten directions coming together:
There are three sections:
first, as stated in the *Sūtra on Rebirth According to One’s Vows*:
“The Buddha-lands of the ten directions are all adorned and pure; according to one’s vows, one shall attain rebirth in them all.”

"In the western direction there is Amitābha Buddha, along with the Bodhisattvas Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta; you should all single-mindedly join your palms and seek to behold them."
Thereupon, the great assembly all followed the Buddha’s exhortation, joining their palms and entreating him with compassion.

At that time, that Buddha emitted a great radiance, and Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta arrived simultaneously; they recited a great divine mantra, whereby all sickness and suffering were entirely eliminated, and everyone was restored to their former state.

However, the spiritual powers of these two Buddhas must likewise be equal; it is simply that Śākyamuni Tathāgata does not manifest his own capabilities, but rather highlights the excellence of the other, desiring that all sentient beings without exception turn toward him in refuge. Therefore, one should understand the underlying intent behind Śākyamuni’s frequent praises of taking refuge here and there.
Therefore, Master Tanyuan, with his mind set on returning to the West, composed a hymn of praise based on the *Mahāyāna Sūtra*, saying:

"The assembly of śrāvakas and bodhisattvas in Sukhāvatī, as well as humans and devas, all possess penetrating wisdom; their physical forms are adorned without distinction, yet they are listed by name only because they follow [the conventions of] other lands."

Your countenance is upright and beyond compare; your exquisite and subtle body is neither human nor celestial. Your body is of the void, an infinite essence; therefore, I prostrate to the One of Equal Power.
Third, regarding the explanation of the intention behind going [to the Buddha]:
there are two parts within this,
the first of which is the explanation of the intention behind going.
II. Explanation through Question and Answer.
First, the question is asked:
"Now I wish to be born in the Pure Land; I do not yet know what the underlying intention for this should be."
He replied:

“I simply wish to swiftly accomplish self-benefit and the benefit of others, so that the benefit of beings may be profound and vast. Through the ten stages of faith and the three levels of worthiness, I shall embrace the True Dharma, realize non-duality, witness Buddha-nature, and clearly understand the true mark of reality.”

Contemplating and illuminating the mind, one perceives the two truths of existence and non-existence, the priority and sequence of cause and effect, the superiority and inferiority of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), the three patiences (*kṣānti*) and the three paths (*mārga*), the unimpeded diamond-like state, and the realization of great *nirvāṇa*. The Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*) operates with vast capacity; desiring to abide for infinite time, it is for the sake of exhausting the boundless ocean of birth and death.
There were three rounds of questions. He asked:
"Those who wish to be born in the Pure Land and intend to benefit sentient beings—"
If that were so, those sentient beings who have been rescued would now be present here.
Having already been able to give rise to this mind, they should simply remain here to rescue suffering sentient beings.
"For what reason, having attained this mind, do you first vow to be born in a pure land?
It seems as though you are abandoning sentient beings to seek the bliss of bodhi for yourself.
He replied:
"This interpretation is inconsistent. Why?
As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:"
"It is like two people who both see their father, mother, and kinsmen submerged in a deep abyss.
One person goes straight in and exerts all his strength to rescue them; failing in his strength, he sinks along with them.
The other person runs far away to a boat, boards it, and comes to their rescue, so that they all emerge from the peril together."
The Bodhisattva is likewise: when he has not yet resolved his mind [for enlightenment], his wandering in the cycle of birth and death is no different from that of ordinary beings;

but once he has already resolved his mind for Bodhi, he first vows to be reborn in a Pure Land, takes up the boat of great compassion, and, riding upon unimpeded eloquence, enters the ocean of birth and death to ferry and deliver sentient beings.
Second, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* further states:

"When Bodhisattvas are born in the Pure Land, possessing great supernormal powers and unimpeded eloquence, even when they teach and transform sentient beings, they are still unable to cause those beings to give rise to goodness, eliminate evil, increase their path, and advance in their stages according to the Bodhisattvas' intentions."
"If one were to provide salvation while remaining in this defiled land, such benefit would be lacking; it would be like forcing a chicken into water—how could it possibly remain dry?
Third, the *Praise of the Mahāyāna Sūtra* states:

"The bodhisattvas of the Land of Peace and Bliss can indeed proclaim according to their wisdom; regarding all things as their own, they have abandoned the notion of 'mine,' and are as pure as a lotus flower, unsullied by dust."

Coming and going, advancing and halting, they are like a boat floating upon the water; making peace and security their primary concern, they abandon preferences and aversions. Regarding self and others as empty, they sever dualistic thoughts, yet they hold aloft the torch of wisdom to illuminate the long night.

The three vidyās and six supernatural powers are all perfected; the Bodhisattva’s myriad practices are observed with the eye of wisdom. Such merit is boundless and immeasurable; therefore, with a sincere heart, I vow to be reborn there.
Within the ninth major section, there are two rounds of analysis:
first, the contrast between suffering and happiness, and good and evil;
second, the comparison of the lengths of life for oneself and others.
Within the first section, there are two parts:
first, the pairing of suffering and happiness, and good and evil;
second, citing the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* as scriptural evidence.
First, regarding the statement that suffering and happiness, as well as good and evil, are relative:

although there are both the two retributions of suffering and happiness within this Sahā world, it is characterized by a constant preponderance of suffering over happiness. In its most severe form, beings are tormented by the agonies of the three miserable realms;
in its lighter forms, humans and devas are beset by a continuous succession of warfare and disease, which has persisted without interruption for distant eons.
Even if there is a slight pleasure for humans or devas, it is like foam or a flash of lightning—arising and ceasing rapidly; therefore, it is said to be nothing but suffering and nothing but evil.

In the Pure Land of Amitābha, the water, birds, and forest trees constantly emit the sounds of the Dharma, clearly proclaiming the Way and teaching; they are perfectly pure and capable of leading beings to awakening and entry.
Second, citing sacred teachings as proof.
The *Treatise on the Pure Land* states:

"Those humans and devas from the ten directions who are born in that land are no different from the Bodhisattvas of Pure Mind; and these Bodhisattvas of Pure Mind are ultimately identical to the Bodhisattvas of the higher stages in attaining the patience of quiescence (*śānti-kṣānti*), and thus they never again regress."
Furthermore, citing the forty-eight vows of the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*, there are five instances of great benefit.
First, the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states:
"If there are beings from the ten directions among devas and humans who come to be born in my land and they are not all of a true golden color, may I not attain perfect enlightenment."

Second, he said: "If those from the ten directions among devas and humans who come to be born in my land should have different forms and colors, whether beautiful or ugly, I shall not attain perfect enlightenment.

Third, he said: 'If those from the ten directions among devas and humans who come to be born in my land should not obtain the knowledge of past lives, even to the extent of not knowing the events of hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of kalpas, I shall not attain perfect enlightenment.

Fourth, he said: 'If those from the ten directions among devas and humans who come to be born in my land should not obtain the supernormal power of the divine ear, even to the extent of not hearing and fully retaining what hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddhas have spoken, I shall not attain perfect enlightenment.'"

Fifth, if those from the heavens and the human realms of the ten directions who come to be born in my land do not attain the knowledge of others' minds—even to the extent of failing to know the mental thoughts of beings in hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddha-lands—I shall not attain perfect enlightenment.
If one were to discuss the matters of benefit in that land, it would be difficult to describe them in full.
One should simply aspire to be born there; it is truly inconceivable.
Therefore, in that direction, there is only goodness and only bliss, with neither suffering nor evil.
Second, regarding the clarification of the length and brevity of lifespan:
in this region, the maximum span of life does not exceed one hundred years; within those hundred years, there are few who reach it and many who fall short.
Some die prematurely in their youth, even as infants; others suffer miscarriages or stillbirths. Why is this so?
It is because the causes created by sentient beings are diverse; therefore, the retributions they receive cannot be uniform.
Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
"When one performs an action that is black, the retribution is also black;
when one performs an action that is white, the retribution is also white."
"The same applies to pure and mixed [karma].
Furthermore, according to the *Jingdu pusa jing* (Sūtra on the Bodhisattva Pure Attainment):
"When human life expectancy is one hundred years, half is consumed by night; this is equivalent to reducing it by fifty years."

Within the span of fifty years, from fifteen onward one does not yet know good or evil, and from eighty onward one is clouded by senility and physically frail; thus, one undergoes the suffering of old age.

Beyond this, there are only fifteen years remaining; during that time, externally, one will be oppressed by royal officials, forced into long expeditions and distant garrisons, or imprisoned in dungeons;
internally, one will be entangled in the various affairs of family fortune and misfortune, feeling restless and anxious, constantly seeking more than enough.
If one calculates in this manner, how much time could possibly remain to cultivate the work of the Path?
Reflecting thus, is it not truly lamentable?
How can one not feel weary [of worldly existence]?
Furthermore, that sutra states:

"In the course of a single day and night in this world, a person undergoes eight hundred and forty million moments of thought (*citta-kṣaṇa*). If one gives rise to an evil thought for a single moment, one receives an evil body;
if one gives rise to evil thoughts for ten moments, one obtains ten births in evil bodies."
If one harbors evil thoughts for a hundred moments, one will receive a hundred evil bodies.

Calculating within the single form of a single sentient being, if one harbors evil thoughts for a hundred years, that evil will fill the three thousandfold world system, and one will receive those evil bodies accordingly.
As it is with unwholesome dharmas, so it is with wholesome dharmas.
If one gives rise to a single thought of goodness, one receives a single wholesome body;
if one gives rise to a hundred thoughts of goodness, one receives a hundred wholesome bodies.
"If, within the single lifetime of a single sentient being, one contemplates goodness for a hundred years, the virtuous bodies [of merit] will fill three thousand lands.

If one can contemplate Amitābha Buddha for ten years or five years, or even for many years, one shall subsequently be born in the Land of Immeasurable Life. Therein, one immediately attains the Dharma-body of the Pure Land, which is as inexhaustible as the sands of the Ganges and inconceivable.
Now, as this is a defiled land where life is brief and the retribution of one's lifespan does not extend far,
if one is born in the Pure Land of Amitābha, one’s lifespan will be long and inconceivable.
Therefore, the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Life* says:
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"For what reason is that Buddha named Amitābha?
Śāriputra!..."

The humans and devas from the ten directions who are reborn in that land have lifespans lasting for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, equal to those of the Buddha; therefore, he is named Amitābha.
"Each person should weigh this great benefit for themselves and aspire to be reborn there.
Furthermore, the *Sūtra of the Honored Emperor Good King* states:

"Should there be a person who studies the Way and desires to be reborn in the Western Land of Amitābha Buddha, they should maintain mindfulness day and night for one day, or two days, or three days, or four days, or five days, up to six or seven days."

Furthermore, if one should later wish to repent for those [transgressions], upon hearing me speak of the merits of this virtuous king, at the time when their life is about to end, eight bodhisattvas will all fly there to welcome and take that person to the land of Amitābha Buddha in the western direction, from which they shall never again return.
From this point onward, he further cites verses from the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* as proof, praising them thus:

"There are sentient beings born into peace and bliss, all fully endowed with the thirty-two marks; their wisdom is perfected as they enter the profound Dharma, thoroughly elucidating the essentials of the Path without obstruction."

According to the sharpness or dullness of their faculties, they achieve patience; through the three types of patience up to the ineffable, they possess constant mastery over the five supernormal powers of past lives, and until they reach Buddhahood, they never again fall into the evil realms.

Except for those born in other worlds of the five turbidities, who manifest as being like the Great Muni; those born in the Land of Peace and Bliss achieve great benefit—therefore, with a sincere heart, I vow to be born there.
Within the tenth major section, there are two parts of analysis:
first, citing analogies from the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* to provide proof and verification;
second, explaining the meaning of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*).
First, regarding the citation of analogies from the *Mahā-sūtra* to provide authentic proof:

there are no Buddhas of the ten directions who do not exhort [beings] to take refuge in the West; there are no Bodhisattvas of the ten directions who do not share in rebirth there; and among humans and devas of the ten directions, there are none whose intent is not to return there in unison. Therefore, one knows this to be an inconceivable matter.
Therefore, the *Praise of the Great Sutra* says:

"The Amitābha of infinite spiritual power is praised by the immeasurable Buddhas of the ten directions; from the Buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the eastern quarter, countless bodhisattvas all go there to pay their respects."

Furthermore, they also made offerings to the great assembly of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas in the Land of Peace and Bliss, listening to and receiving the Dharma teachings as they proclaimed the transformation of beings; it was likewise so in the other nine directions.
Second, regarding the explanation of the meaning of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*):
since all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, every individual possesses the aspiration to attain Buddhahood.
However, based on the karma of their practiced cultivation, until one full ten thousand kalpas have passed, they still have not emerged from the realm of fire and cannot escape saṃsāra.
Therefore, the Noble One, out of compassion for these long-lasting sufferings, exhorted them to turn westward so that great benefit might be achieved.
However, the merit of dedication does not exceed six types. What are these six?
First, dedicating all the karmic deeds one has cultivated toward Amitābha.
Having arrived in that land, one again attains the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) to deliver and sustain sentient beings; this is precisely "non-abiding on the path.
Second, turning the cause toward the fruit;
third, turning the lower toward the higher.
4. Turning from the slow toward the swift, which is precisely not abiding in the world;
5. Turning to bestow upon sentient beings, directing compassionate thoughts toward the good;
6. Turning to enter [the path] and eliminate the mind of discrimination.
The merit of dedication accomplishes only these six.
Therefore, the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states:
"Any sentient beings who are born in my land will naturally advance and transcend the practices of the various stages belonging to ordinary ranks."
"Once one has attained the path of Buddhahood, there will be no further difficulty of regression.
Thus, the *Mahāvaipulya-sūtra-stava* says:

'The Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas of the Land of Peace and Bliss have no equal in this world; even if Śākyamuni’s unimpeded great eloquence were to employ every possible metaphor, it could only show a small fraction [of their qualities].'"

The most lowly beggar is equal to a sovereign king, and the sovereign king is further compared to a Wheel-Turning King; thus it is successively extended up to the six heavens, each stage being analogous to the one preceding it, just as at the beginning.

To compare his physical form and appearance to others, he is many thousands of millions of times beyond their kind; all this is brought about by the power of his vows as a treasury of Dharma. I bow my head in prostration to him of great mental power.
Within the eleventh great gate, there is a brief twofold analysis:
first, exhorting all sentient beings to rely upon spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) with the intention of heading toward the West;
second, distinguishing the superiority and inferiority of the conditions for rebirth after death.
First, regarding the exhortation to rely upon spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*):
according to the *Dharmapada*, one acts as a spiritual friend to sentient beings. As the Bodhisattva Ratnaprabha addressed the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!..."
"What is meant by 'spiritual friend' (kalyāṇamitra)? The Buddha said:

"A spiritual friend is one who can expound the profound Dharma—namely, emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; the equality of all phenomena; the absence of karma and its retribution; the absence of cause and effect; ultimate suchness (tathatā); and abiding in the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi)."
Nevertheless, within ultimate emptiness, they vigorously establish all dharmas;
such are spiritual friends.
Spiritual friends are your parents, for they nurture your bodhi-bodies.
A virtuous friend is your eye, for they enable you to see all paths of good and evil;
a virtuous friend is your great ship, for they transport you across the ocean of birth and death;
a virtuous friend is your rope, for they can pull you out from birth and death.
Furthermore, he exhorted them that although they might act as spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) to sentient beings, they must return to the West. Why is this?
It is because dwelling in this realm of fire involves many favorable and unfavorable conditions; there are many instances of falling back or sinking, and it is difficult to escape.
Therefore, Śāriputra, having resolved his mind upon this and practiced the bodhisattva path for sixty kalpas, he encountered an evil friend who begged for his eyes;
due to these circumstances, he subsequently regressed.

Therefore, know that the cultivation of the path within the realm of fire is exceedingly difficult; thus, I urge you to take refuge in the Western Land. Once rebirth there is attained, the three trainings will naturally advance and the myriad practices will be universally perfected.
Therefore, the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states:
"In Amitābha’s Pure Land, there is not even a hair's breadth of ground for committing evil.
Second, we shall next distinguish between the superior and inferior births that sentient beings undergo after death.

When the sentient beings of this realm reach the end of their lifespan and die, there are none who do not ride upon the two karmas of good and evil; they are constantly led by the jailers of destiny and, through deluded craving and afflictions, undergo rebirth together.
Since countless kalpas past, they have been unable to escape this state.

If one can give rise to faith and take refuge in the Pure Land, applying oneself with focused diligence, then at the moment of death, Amitābha Buddha, together with the holy assembly of Avalokiteśvara and others, will come to welcome them upon a radiant lotus pedestal.
The practitioner follows with joy, joining his palms as he ascends the platform; in a mere moment he arrives, experiencing nothing but happiness until he attains Buddhahood.
Furthermore, all sentient beings create different karmas, which are of three types:
superior, middling, and inferior; there are none who do not go before Yama to receive judgment.

If one can believe in the causes and conditions of the Buddha and vow to be born in the Pure Land, dedicating all practiced deeds toward that end, then at the time of death, the Buddha will personally come to welcome them, rather than the King of Death.
Within the twelfth major section, there is one chapter that uses the *Sūtra on the Ten Rebirths* as scriptural evidence to exhort rebirth [in the Pure Land].
As the Buddha taught regarding birth in the land of Amitābha Buddha, he spoke to the great assembly on the contemplation of the body and liberation through right mindfulness.
The *Sūtra on the Ten Rebirths* states:
"Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
'World-Honored One!'"
"How is the method for all sentient beings to contemplate the body?
I pray that you will explain it.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"Regarding the method for observing the body: one does not observe east or west, nor south or north; one does not observe the four intermediate directions, above, or below; one does not observe empty space; one does not observe external conditions, nor internal conditions; one does not observe the physical form of the body, nor its colors or sounds, nor its appearances. One observes only the absence of conditions (*anālambana*); this is the correct and true method for observing the body."
"Apart from this contemplation of the body, if one searches thoroughly throughout the ten directions, there is nowhere else to find a distinct dharma by which one may attain liberation.
The Buddha further addressed Ānanda:
"Simply contemplate the body for yourself; the power of goodness is spontaneous, right mindfulness is spontaneous, and liberation is spontaneous."
Why is this? It is like a person who, through diligence and a straightforward mind, attains right liberation.
Such a person does not seek liberation, yet liberation comes to them spontaneously.
Ānanda again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
If the sentient beings of the world possessed such right mindfulness and liberation, there would be no three evil realms at all—namely, the hells, the hungry ghosts, and the animals."
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“The sentient beings of the world do not attain liberation. Why is this?
All sentient beings are characterized by much falsehood and little reality, lacking even a single moment of right mindfulness.
Due to these causes and conditions, those in the hells are many, while those who attain liberation are few.

For example, suppose there is a person who outwardly manifests filial piety toward his father, mother, and preceptors, yet inwardly harbors unfilial thoughts; who outwardly manifests diligence, yet inwardly harbors insincerity. Although the retribution for such an evil person has not yet arrived, the three miserable realms are not far off.
"Without right mindfulness, one does not attain liberation.
Ānanda spoke again to the Buddha, saying:
"If this is so, what further roots of goodness should be cultivated to attain right liberation?"
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Listen well now!
I shall now speak for you."
There are ten methods for rebirth that can lead to liberation.
What are these ten?

First, by contemplating the body with right mindfulness and constantly maintaining joy, one gives food, drink, and clothing to the Buddha and the Sangha, thereby attaining rebirth in the land of Amitābha Buddha.
Second, with right mindfulness, one bestows sweet, wondrous, and excellent medicine upon a single sick bhikṣu and all sentient beings, thereby being reborn in the land of Amitābha Buddha;
third, with right mindfulness, one does not harm a single living being, maintains compassion for all, and is reborn in the land of Amitābha Buddha;

fourth, with right mindfulness, one upholds the precepts received from a teacher, cultivates pure conduct through clear wisdom, and with a heart always filled with joy, is reborn in the land of Amitābha Buddha.

Fifth, with right mindfulness, being filial and obedient toward one’s parents, reverently serving one’s teachers and elders, and not giving rise to a mind of arrogance, one will be reborn in the land of Amitābha Buddha;

sixth, with right mindfulness, going to the monastic quarters, showing respect to stupas and temples, hearing the Dharma and understanding its single meaning, one will be reborn in the land of Amitābha Buddha;

seventh, with right mindfulness, for the duration of one day and one night, upholding the eight precepts of purification without breaking even a single one, one will be reborn in the land of Amitābha Buddha.

Eighth, those with right mindfulness who, during months of fasting and days of fasting, remain far from their dwellings and constantly visit virtuous teachers, shall be reborn in the land of Amitābha Buddha;

ninth, those with right mindfulness who can always maintain pure precepts, diligently cultivate meditative concentration, protect the Dharma, and refrain from harsh speech—if they practice in this way, they shall be reborn in the land of Amitābha Buddha;

tenth, those with right mindfulness who do not give rise to a mind of slander toward the unsurpassed path, who zealously uphold the pure precepts, and furthermore teach the ignorant to disseminate this sutra and its Dharma, thereby transforming immeasurable sentient beings—all such persons as these shall attain rebirth.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Sāgarameghaprajñā who addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
What marvelous joys and superior matters are there in that land of Amitābha such that all sentient beings wish to be reborn there?"
That Buddha told the Bodhisattva Ocean-Mountain Wisdom:
"You should now stand up, join your palms, straighten your body toward the west, and with right mindfulness contemplate the land of Amitābha Buddha, vowing to behold Amitābha Buddha."
At that time, the entire great assembly also rose and joined their palms, gazing together at Amitābha Buddha.
Then Amitābha Buddha manifested great supernormal powers, emitting a vast radiance that illuminated the body of the Bodhisattva Ocean-Mountain Wisdom.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Sāgaradharabuddhivikrīḍitābhijña and the others beheld the land of Amitābha Buddha; all its magnificent and exquisite adornments were composed entirely of the seven treasures—seven-treasure mountains and seven-treasure lands—where the water-birds and the forest trees constantly emitted the sounds of the Dharma.

In that land, the Wheel of Dharma is turned day after day. The people of that land do not practice external matters, but practice exclusively internal matters; their mouths speak the words of the Vaipulya, their ears hear the sounds of the Vaipulya, and their minds comprehend the meanings of the Vaipulya.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sāgarabuddhivikrīḍitābhijña addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
We who now behold that land perceive its supreme, wondrous benefits to be inconceivable."
"I now vow that all sentient beings shall be reborn there, and thereafter we too shall vow to be born in that land.
The Buddha granted them this prediction, saying:
"Those who possess right view, right mindfulness, and attain right liberation shall all be born there."

If there are good sons or good daughters who, with right faith, accept this sutra and cherish it, and who exhort and guide sentient beings—both those who preach it and those who listen—all shall be reborn in the land of Amitābha Buddha.

If there are such persons as these, from this day forward I shall always cause twenty-five bodhisattvas to protect and sustain them, constantly ensuring that they are free from illness and affliction, so that neither humans nor non-humans may find an opportunity to harm them; whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, they shall always attain peace and security, regardless of day or night.
The Bodhisattva Sāgarabuddhi addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One, I now receive your venerable teaching upon the crown of my head and dare not harbor any doubt.
However, there are sentient beings in the world who frequently slander it and do not believe in this sutra; what will become of such people in the future?”
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Sāgarabuddhivikrāmin:
"In the future, there may be bhikṣus or bhikṣuṇīs in Jambudvīpa who, upon seeing those who read and recite this sutra, will become angry with one another and harbor thoughts of slander."

Because of this slander of the True Dharma, in their present life, these people will encounter various grave and evil illnesses; they will be deficient in their physical faculties, becoming deaf, blind, mute, or speech-impaired; they will suffer from dropsy and demonic possession, finding no peace whether sitting or lying down; they will seek life but cannot find it, and they will seek death but cannot find it.

Or they may even die and fall into hell, where for eighty thousand *kalpas* they undergo great suffering and affliction; for hundreds of thousands of millions of lifetimes, they have never even heard the names of water or food.
After a long time they finally emerge, only to be slaughtered by humans as oxen, horses, pigs, or sheep, undergoing extreme agony.
Later, if they obtain human form, they are always born in lowly places; for hundreds of thousands of millions of lifetimes they lack autonomy and never hear the names of the Triple Gem.
"Therefore, do not preach this sutra among those who lack wisdom and faith.

Having compiled and propagated these merits, may they be bestowed universally upon all; may they first resolve to attain Bodhicitta, together turn toward the Pure Land, and all together realize the Buddha-way.

The *Anrakushū*, Volume Lower. This collection exists in both ancient and modern woodblock editions. Frequently, various editions distinguish between "fish" and "lu" (i.e., misread characters), resulting in minor discrepancies.

It was only upon reaching Master Benli that the teachings of the two former lecturers, Licheng and Yanchang, were inherited; he subsequently produced a work titled *Zhengcuo* (Correcting Errors) to specifically identify and resolve the erroneous passages.
The senior monks of the same quarters, Masters Fǎngshān and Sēngpò, each supplemented its omissions and deficiencies.
It is hoped that this will encounter the source of the River of the Dharma, just as the late Master Běnlì once said:
"One must carefully edit this collected works to carry on the Master’s intention."
As for the phrase "the master," his karmic timing was set for another day; his efforts were not fulfilled, and he passed away in peace.

This senior teacher was the spiritual brother of my former master. My former master also harbored the ambition to edit and carve [this work], and he once requested it of this venerable elder. Having already received your consent, he too passed away in peace shortly after reaching the twilight years of his life.

At the moment when the silk was placed over his mouth, he entrusted this matter to me, his unworthy descendant. Alas! Though I, Pu, am of such a base character that I dare not presume to such a position, I could not refuse his final testament and have thus reluctantly accepted it.

Since then, illusory conditions have been overwhelming and my body has frequently suffered from illness; as the seasons of winter and summer robes have alternated three times and the period of mourning for my parents has concluded, I cannot help but sigh with deep sorrow:
"The two elders have returned to stillness, yet this single volume has not yet been placed upon the wooden tablet. Alas!"
"How could such complications have arisen regarding this matter?
His bequeathed intent was more than clear; though I am but a humble and unworthy person, how could I dare to neglect or set it aside?

Thus, without measuring my own abilities, I have exerted myself in this task. While I relied primarily on the edition prepared by Yanchi Temple, I further collated various printed versions to identify discrepancies, making compromises and revisions—though how could I presume to do so?

Furthermore, I have extracted and corrected the essential points merely for the sake of easy consultation; that I have not been able to fully realize the intentions of these two elders is due to my own unworthiness and lack of ability. I hope that those of like mind from all quarters will edit and supplement this work.
Nanhu: Recorded by the Chan monk Longke Pusu Qin of Huanzhu.
Regarding the two fascicles of the *Anle ji* (Collection on Peaceful Joy) that have been circulated through woodblock printing since the Kwanwon era, there are occasional errors in the text.

I have now gathered several versions from various sources, including those held at Gyōkan-ji in Yokogawa, Sankei-ji in Mizuho, Myōe-ji in Umeo, Shin'en-ji in Negoro, and Echin-ji in Kurodani, and have compared them as occasion arose. Where the correct reading was clear, I decisively adopted one and rejected the others, treating them as a single unified text. As for those passages that remain ambiguous and cannot be definitively resolved, I have left them blank, entrusting their determination to future scholars.
Furthermore, the punctuation marks and the four tones are added as sub-scripts to facilitate readers in pronouncing them easily.

On the twenty-fifth day of the first month of the eleventh year of the Eiroku era (the Wuyin year), the monk Yishan of the Zenlian Society solicited contributions for the carving of this woodblock edition.
